articles.summary: An approved supplier list is the master record of who you're allowed to buy from, by part, by category, and by spend threshold. At most companies it's a stale spreadsheet nobody trusts. Here's how to fix it.
articles.title: Approved Supplier List: How to Build One, Keep It Current, and Actually Use It

articles.summary: Most procurement KPIs are vanity metrics that look thorough but don't predict real performance, and here are the seven that actually do.
articles.title: Procurement KPIs That Actually Predict Performance

articles.summary: Incoterms are the 11 standard ICC trade terms (Incoterms 2020) that define who pays for what and where risk transfers between buyer and seller in international shipping.
articles.title: What Are Incoterms? The 2020 Rules, Explained for Buyers

articles.summary: Lead time in procurement is the elapsed time between placing a purchase order and the goods arriving at your dock, ready to use. The number on the BOM is almost always wrong.
articles.title: Lead Time in Procurement: Why the Number on the BOM Is Lying to You

articles.summary: Source-to-pay vs procure-to-pay isn't really a head-to-head, it's a scope question, and most manufacturing teams don't need a full S2P suite.
articles.title: Source-to-Pay vs Procure-to-Pay: The Real Difference (And Why Most Teams Don't Need S2P)

articles.summary: An RFQ (Request for Quotation) is the formal document a buyer sends to suppliers asking for a price, lead time, and terms on a defined scope. The mechanics are simple. Running RFQs well is not.
articles.title: What Is an RFQ?

articles.summary: An open purchase order is any PO that's been issued but not fully received, billed, or closed. At most companies, that list is full of risk nobody is watching. Here's how to read it and what to do about it.
articles.title: Open Purchase Orders: What They Are, Why They Pile Up, and How to Manage Them

articles.summary: A 3-way match compares the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the supplier invoice before AP pays. When all three agree, the invoice gets paid. When they don't, somebody has to figure out why.
articles.title: 3-Way Match: The AP Process That Catches What Procurement Missed

articles.summary: A bill of materials (BOM) is the structured list of every part, sub-assembly, and raw material that goes into a finished product. The list itself is easy. Keeping it accurate as engineering and procurement diverge is the actual job.
articles.title: Bill of Materials: What a BOM Really Tracks (and Why It's Always Slightly Wrong)
